prose: Rain slides down the tall black panes in unbroken sheets. The fire shifts, a coal settling. Nell's snore catches, then resumes. Sir Julian's signet ring is turned wrong-way-round on his finger—a detail a man in his station would correct if he noticed, which means he does not notice, or does not care to. Lady Thorne's grey gloves are motionless. Beaumont has not moved since you entered. Your own sherry sits where you left it.

input: I let the silence go on a little past the point of comfort — I find people tell you a great deal in the space where they expect a question. Then I set my untouched sherry on the mantel and cross, unhurried, to the fender, where I crouch and hold the back of my hand out to the old spaniel. She wakes, sniffs, thumps her tail once. "Handsome old girl," I say, without turning round. "Spaniels were always the honest ones — no talent for pretending to be pleased. What's her name, Sir Julian? I find a man's dog tells you more about him than his portrait ever does." I stay crouched, my back to him, my attention entirely on the animal, giving him all the room in the world to answer easily. It is a small question. That is why I am asking it.

She stirs, blinks, sniffs once—then the tail thumps against the hearth rug. A single, heavy beat. I stay there, back to the room, and let the silence stretch. Sir Julian fills it. "Ah, you've found her weakness — she'll take to anyone who'll scratch behind the ear. The naming of her, now, that's my wife's territory. She claimed the honour and defends it jealously. My dear, you'd better remind the inspector — I've called her 'old girl' for so long I've quite forgotten what's on her papers." Lady Thorne says nothing. The clock ticks. A draft from the rain-lashed windows stirs the fire. I keep my hand where it is, waiting on the spaniel's answer.

input: I don't turn round. I keep my hand on the spaniel's warm skull, and I let Sir Julian's deflection hang unanswered in the air for a moment — long enough that everyone hears it land on Lady Thorne rather than on him. Then, still to the dog, mild as milk: "Yes, do tell me, Lady Thorne. I should like to hear you say it." Only now do I glance up, and I look not at her but at Beaumont by the door — one brief, courteous, professional flick of the eyes, the look of a man simply noting who else is in the room. Then back to the dog, waiting.
prose: The silence holds. The fire shifts. Nell's ribs rise and fall under my hand. Sir Julian's chuckle has already faded; the leather of his chair creaks once as he settles deeper. Lady Thorne's voice, when it comes, is precise, dry, unhurried: "Nell. After my mother's favourite character, if you can believe such sentiment in a Thorne. She answers to it when it suits her — which is rarely, and only for food." The spaniel sighs. Sir Julian's right hand finds the sherry glass on the side table. He says warmly, "There — you see the kind of woman I married, Inspector? Sentiment through and through, and she'll deny it to her dying breath. Nell suits her, though, I'll grant my wife that much. She never did answer to anything else." I let the deflection land. The clock ticks. The rain streams. My hand stays on the dog's skull. I glance up. Beaumont stands by the door, his gaze dropping from the neutral point above the mantel to track Sir Julian's right hand closing on the sherry glass — holds there a half-second longer than a servant's glance should — then lifts back to the wall. A brief, courteous flick of the eyes, then I return to the spaniel. Lady Thorne's voice, from behind me: "Nell." A pause. Then, dry and precise: "My husband exaggerates, Inspector — but only slightly." The spaniel shifts under my hand, and I wait.

input: I give Nell a last scratch and rise, unhurried, my knees cracking in the quiet. I take my sherry from the mantel at last but only turn the glass in my fingers, still not drinking. "Charming," I say. "A house with a dog in it is never quite lost." I drift — not toward Sir Julian, but toward the portraits on the far wall, hands behind my back, the very picture of a man admiring the paint. I stop before what is plainly a christening portrait: a younger Lady Thorne, an infant in white lace, a clergyman. "Your boy," I say, warmly, without turning. "Edward, isn't it? Handsome christening. I do like a country parson — they marry you and bury you and christen your children and remember every word of it fifty years on." A pause, light as a feather. "Who was yours, Sir Julian? The man who did the honours here. I collect country clergymen the way some men collect stamps."
prose: I turn the sherry glass in my fingers — cool, still untouched — and let the silence breathe. A coal settles in the grate. Then Sir Julian's voice rolls out from the wing chair, warm and expansive: "Ah, you're a collector — that explains a great deal about you, Inspector. Most men collect butterflies or first editions, and you collect parsons. Now, the christening — I remember the sermon, because the poor fellow went on for forty minutes on the meaning of a name, and Edward howled through every second of it. Handsome boy, but he had lungs on him. The vicar himself — dear old boy, white hair, voice like a bell — you'll think me terrible, but we've had two changes of cloth since we came to Thornfield and I muddle them. My wife keeps the parish roster in her head far better than I do. But tell me — who's the prize specimen in your collection? The one you'd put under glass."

input: I laugh, quietly, genuinely — give him that much; it's a good redirect and I've a professional's respect for a good redirect. "The prize of my collection," I say, turning at last to face the room, "isn't a clergyman at all. It's a death certificate. I collect the ones that were never filed." I let that sit exactly one heartbeat, mild as ever, my eyes on the fire and not on him. "But that's shop talk, and I'm keeping you from your evening. Do you know, before I forget —" I finally lift the sherry as if to drink, then don't, "— a colleague of mine was out in Tangier this spring. Filthy climate, he said. Fever season. Carries people off before the paperwork can catch them." Now I look at Sir Julian, pleasantly, the way you'd look at any man across a fire. "Were you ever out that way? I only ask because you've the look of a man who's seen a hot country. It leaves a mark, Tangier. On some men more than others."
prose: I laugh — a quiet sound, genuine enough to have cost something. The fire pops. Nell's ears twitch. I let the line sit, one beat, face turned to the flames; the clock ticks through it. Then I turn, lift the sherry as if to drink, and set it back down untouched. Sir Julian's eyes catch the motion — a flicker, no more. I look at him then, pleasantly, across the hearth. He laughs back, expansive, a performance of warmth that doesn't reach his eyes. 'Death certificates! My dear Inspector, you're a grimmer man than I credited — I'd have sworn you for a butterfly collector, and here you are keeping mortality under glass. That's a hobby for a man with a strong stomach.' He pauses; the leather creaks. 'Tangier, though — yes. I won't pretend otherwise; you've caught me out. A few weeks there, on my way back. Enough to learn that the light does something peculiar to a man's head — makes every street look like a painting that hasn't dried yet. And the heat — good Lord, the heat. You learn to move at the country's pace or it moves through you. I came back with a tan, a taste for mint tea, and a permanent distrust of noon. But your colleague — now I'm curious. Did he bring back anything worse than stories?' His signet ring is still turned wrong-way-round. The firelight catches his face. Nell thumps her tail once against the fender, settles. The rain drives on.

Then I turn to Lady Thorne, and my manner changes — warmer, almost gentle, the way one is careful with the recently bereaved. "Forgive me, Lady Thorne. I've been monopolising your husband and neglecting you, and it's you I most wanted to ask. When Sir Julian came home this spring — from his travels — how did he seem to you? A wife sees what the world misses. Was he quite himself?" I hold her eyes, only her eyes, with great courtesy. "I ask because a man can come back from a hot country very changed. In thirty years of service — has the master ever, once, since he came home this spring, called you by the wrong name?"

input: "Once," I say. "Thank you, Beaumont. A man like you wouldn't have said it if it weren't true, and wouldn't have said a word more than he had to. You've done your duty and no more, and no one in this room can fault you for it." I let him have that — he will need it. Then I reach into my breast pocket, and the room knows before my hand comes out that the evening has changed. I take out a photograph, stiff-backed, eight months old, and I do not brandish it. I simply walk to the side table, set it down in the pool of lamplight where every person here can see it, and step back. It is a photograph of a man. Thin, fair, a scar through one eyebrow, taken on a hospital verandah under a hard bright sky. On the reverse, in a colonial registrar's hand: Sir Julian Thorne, deceased, Tangier. "That is Sir Julian Thorne," I say, to the room, to all of them at once, gently, without triumph. "He died of fever eight months ago, and no one told England." I do not look at the man in the wing chair. I look at Lady Thorne. "The only question left in this room is which of you is going to tell me the truth first — and I would think very carefully, Lady Thorne, about how little time the second one to speak will have left to bargain with."

Beaumont's back is a rod of mahogany. He does not blink. Sir Julian rises from the wing chair, crosses to the side table in the pool of lamplight, leans over the photograph. His thumb finds the signet ring on his little finger and turns it a quarter rotation as he straightens. He says, "Now, Inspector — you've been conducting my wake without so much as offering me a seat at it, and that's very poor form. Let me see this photograph that's got you so convinced I'm a dead man. I should like to know what I looked like before the fever carried me off — one doesn't often get the chance to read one's own obituary, and I'm dashed if I'll waste the opportunity from across the room." His voice is expansive, warm, faintly incredulous. Lady Thorne's hands stay folded in her lap. She does not look at the man by the table. She says, "You've said a great deal, Inspector. I would hear what it is you're asking — plainly, please." Her voice is measured, courteous. And I hold her eyes, and I do not look away. The man by the table is a dead man holding a dead man's photograph, and I will not give him the dignity of my attention.

input: I let the man by the table talk, and I do not so much as glance at him. I keep my eyes on Lady Thorne, and when I speak it is to her alone, quiet, almost kind, as if the two of us were the only people in the county. "Plainly, then. That photograph is registered with the consul in Tangier. There is a grave. There is a ship's manifest with your name on it, three weeks after your husband was already in the ground — travelling home, Lady Thorne, from a country you have just heard your companion admit he visited. The rope is already woven. The only thing not yet decided is how many necks are in it." I pause, and I gentle my voice further, because this is the moment and cruelty would waste it. "You did not kill your husband. Fever did. Whatever you did after was done by a widow with a hated cousin at the gate and nothing of her own. A jury can be made to understand a frightened woman. It cannot be made to forgive a woman who chose, tonight, in front of a policeman, to keep lying for the man who is wearing her dead husband's ring. He cannot save you. He cannot even save himself. So I will ask you once, and then the offer closes and I stop being kind: who is the man standing at that table?"

input: "Thank you, Lady Thorne," I say, and I mean it, and I let her hear that I will keep the side of the bargain I have just made. I do not let her answer him. I step once, unhurried, to place myself between her chair and the side table — between the widow and the man in her husband's ring — and only then do I turn, at last, to face him fully. The charm has nowhere left to go and we both know it. "It's finished," I tell him, not unkindly. "She has said it, the photograph says it, and in a moment Beaumont will say it, because you called him the wrong name and a man like Beaumont has spent thirty years unable to lie even to spare himself. There is a car at the end of the drive and two men in it who came up from London with me. You can walk to it with your dignity, or you can make the last thing anyone remembers of 'Sir Julian Thorne' a scene on a wet carpet. I'd think about the ring, if I were you — whose it is, and how it will look, still on your finger, when they take it off you." I keep my hands loose and visible. I am not a large man and he is cornered, and cornered men do the stupidest thing available to them. "Beaumont," I say, without taking my eyes off the impostor, "your master is dead these eight months, and none of what happens now is any failure of yours. But I think you have known there was something in this house that oughtn't to be, for longer than you have let yourself say. You may say it now. What is the man in front of you?"
prose: The thanks land as a genuine thing, and I let her hear that in the weight I give the words. Then I step — once, unhurried — and plant myself between the wing chair and the side table. My back is to the mantel now, and Lady Thorne is behind me, and the impostor has to look at me if he wants to reach her. He does not. He is still looking at the photograph on the side table, or at nothing, or at the space where his charm used to live. I turn to face him fully, and I deliver the case in a flat, unsparing voice — the photograph, the car, the men from London, the choice between a walk and a scene on a wet carpet. I mention the ring, and I keep my hands loose and visible. Then, without shifting my gaze from him, I say to Beaumont: "Your master is dead these eight months, and none of what happens now is any failure of yours. But I think you have known there was something in this house that oughtn't to be, for longer than you have let yourself say. You may say it now. What is the man in front of you?" Beaumont's gaze lifts from the middle distance and settles on the man by the side table. For the first time all evening, he meets his eyes. "I do not know this man, sir." The voice is flat, final, stripped of thirty-one years of composure. A faint roughness on the word 'know' — the only imperfection in a lifetime of service. The impostor's response comes quick, expansive, a beat too fast — he tells Beaumont not to answer, challenges my procedure, appeals to the butler's dignity. But the words are already hollow. For a long moment, the impostor stands motionless. The charm has nowhere left to go. Then, without warning, he lunges for the door — a desperate, clumsy dash, the velvet smoking jacket flaring. I am already moving, stepping into his path, one hand catching his shoulder, the other gripping his arm. He struggles, but I hold him firm. The impostor goes still. His breath comes in ragged gasps. Slowly, he raises his left hand and works the signet ring from his finger — the ring turned the wrong way, the ring that was never his. He holds it out, not to me, not to anyone, and lets it fall. It strikes the Persian carpet with a soft thud. The mantel clock ticks. The rain streams down the black windows. Nell, the spaniel, whines once and is silent. Sir Julian Thorne says: "Beaumont — don't answer that. The Inspector is asking you to name a man you've poured sherry for twice, as though thirty years in this house gives you some particular authority on who walks through its doors. It doesn't, and you've earned better than to be made a witness at someone else's arraignment. And you, Inspector — you've a photograph, a motorcar at the end of my drive, and two men who came up from London. If that constitutes a case, it belongs before a magistrate — not in my drawing room, and not in the mouth of a man who's served this family longer than you've worn that coat."

input: "A magistrate," I agree, mildly, keeping my grip. "Yes. That's exactly where this is going, and you'll have every inch of the law you're suddenly so fond of. But not from that chair, and not with that ring on the floor of another man's house." I raise my voice, just once, toward the tall doors: "Marsh. Ellery." And I hear the front door, and the wet tread of two men coming down the hall. I do not let go of him until they are in the room and their hands are where mine were. Only then do I step back, and stoop, and pick the fallen ring up off the Persian carpet with my handkerchief, and hold it a moment in the lamplight — the small gold circle that started all of this. "Take him to the car," I say. "Gently. He's given us no trouble worth the name." Then, when the room is quieter, I go to Lady Thorne, and I crouch to her level the way I crouched to the dog an hour ago, and I speak so only she can hear. "You did the one thing tonight that a jury will remember. Hold to it. I'll stand up and say you told me the truth when it cost you everything to tell it." I rise. I look, last, at Beaumont — still by the door, thirty-one years and a dead master heavy on him. "Sit down, man," I say, gently. "Before you fall. Your service is over for tonight, and there's no shame anywhere in this room that belongs to you."

Marsh and Ellery come down the hall and into the light, their faces set. I do not let go until their hands are where mine were. He passes between them without a word. I step back. I stoop. The ring lies on the carpet where it fell — I lift it through the handkerchief, turn it once in the lamplight. Then I give the order, quiet, final. They take him out. The front door closes. The house settles. I cross to Lady Thorne, crouch beside her chair. Her hands are still in her lap. I lean in and speak low, the words for her alone. She does not move. I hold her gaze a beat longer, then rise. Beaumont stands by the door, his spine still a rod of mahogany, his face a mask worn thin. I tell him to sit. He does not move. Then his knees give, and he lowers himself into the chair by the fire, slowly, like a man who has forgotten how.

Hold to it. I'll stand up and say you told me the truth when it cost you everything to tell it." He rises and turns to Beaumont. "Sit down, man. Before you fall. Your service is over for tonight, and there's no shame anywhere in this room that belongs to you." Beaumont's jaw works once. He does not speak. After a moment he moves to a chair near the fire and sits, his hands resting on his knees. The mantel clock ticks. The rain streams down the black windows. The photograph of the real Sir Julian Thorne remains on the side table, propped against the decanter. Inspector Vane straightens up, standing tall.

Sir Julian Thorne says: "The gutter on the east wing — it'll go in the next storm. Someone should see to it."
